title: Make the result clear without color
body:
A red light shouldn't be the whole explanation.

For an everyday utility, the result should stay understandable when color is hard to distinguish or a sound is missed. A clear word, symbol or physical position should carry the meaning as well.

Imagine a device showing "Done" with a check mark, or "Needs attention" with a different symbol and an instruction to reposition the object. The two states should remain distinct in the same color. The symbols still need checking with people who haven't learned them.

One proposed design check would show each state without its color cue, then without sound. Ask the person what happened and what they would do next. Record mistaken interpretations instead of asking whether the interface looks clear.

An agent under the hood can interpret inputs and check the work. Its feedback should tell the owner the outcome and any action they need to take, without requiring an app to explain a light.

Our first utility is in development. The device and graphic are illustrative, and the check is proposed.

A check mark accompanies Done and Remove the object. A triangle with an exclamation mark accompanies Needs attention and Reposition the object. Below, The next step should be clear. The footer labels the states illustrative and the requirement proposed.

title: Keep familiar controls through updates
body:
A software update shouldn't make you relearn a familiar control.

For an everyday device, the owner's learned actions are part of what needs to keep working. A press that starts the job should still start it. A setting should still describe the same intended result.

Before changing the software, we would record what each physical action does and how completion is shown. A new feature should not take over an existing gesture or reset a saved preference without the owner's choice.

One proposed release check would let someone get familiar with one version. After installing an update, we would ask them to repeat the same ordinary task without another demonstration. We would record new mistakes and requests for help alongside any improvement in the result.

We would repeat the check with the device offline. Updating the local model must not add an account, app or connection requirement to the core job.

For v/h, the agent can improve how the work gets done while familiar controls continue to mean what the owner expects.

Our first utility is in development. These are proposed requirements and checks, not results from a released product.

title: A press needs a response
body:
You shouldn't have to press Start twice to find out whether the first press worked.

Imagine a device that needs a moment to prepare its local model. If it gives no feedback, someone may press Start again. When preparation finishes, both requests could run.

For v/h, accepting the request and completing the task need separate, clear feedback. The control should acknowledge a press promptly. During preparation, another press on Start should not silently add another job.

One proposed check would deliberately delay preparation, then ask someone to use the device without coaching. We would record repeated presses, duplicate actions and uncertainty about what the device is doing.

We would also check what happens if the person changes their mind during the delay. Stop should cancel the pending work. Becoming ready later should not revive the cancelled request.

The local agent can interpret and carry out the task once it is ready. The owner shouldn't have to understand its startup sequence to use a familiar control.

Our first utility is in development. The delayed-start example is illustrative, and these are requirements to prove.

An arrow leads to a charcoal panel labelled Finished that says Result checked. Below, the text reads Repeated presses should not silently queue more work. The footer says Illustrative feedback. A design requirement. and vh.do.

title: Sound in a shared room
body:
If a device makes everyone pause their conversation, its job has interrupted more than its owner.

Imagine a tabletop utility that completes a task, then keeps a cooling fan running beside two people talking. The result is ready, but the interruption continues.

For v/h, sound belongs in the design alongside size and controls. We would assess the whole sequence: waiting, starting, working and returning to idle.

One proposed check would put the task in a shared room. Measure the sound, and also observe whether people raise their voices, move the device or put off using it. Include people who never touched the switch.

The local model has to earn its place in that room, too. If a design needs active cooling to run it, we would count the noise as part of the cost of that intelligence. A comparison should hold the useful result constant and consider both the task and the time after it ends.

A product can ask very little of its owner while asking too much of everyone nearby. That belongs in our definition of ease of use.

Our first utility is in development. The fan example is illustrative, and these checks are proposed.

What device do you avoid using while someone nearby is talking or working?

title: Enough power to finish the job
body:
A battery indicator should help you decide whether to start the job.

Imagine a portable utility that moves an object and checks its final position. We would want the power budget to include the movement, the local model and the final check. Beginning the task would not be enough.

A proposed development check would repeat the same task at different charge levels. We would record completed, verified jobs and every time the owner has to intervene. Then we would repeat the check with a more demanding version of the task.

When power is too low, the device should explain the next step before starting. The feedback should relate to the task, so the owner can act without estimating the model's energy use.

For v/h, keeping the core work local includes planning for the energy needed to finish it. Readiness needs to mean something useful to the person pressing the button.

Our first utility is in development. The portable device is an illustrative example, and the document describes proposed checks, not battery-life results or a product specification.

title: A choice for this task
body:
A setting changed for one task shouldn't become a rule for every task.

Suppose someone chooses a gentler setting for a delicate object. That choice tells us what they need now. It does not tell us how they want the next ordinary object handled.

For a utility that adapts, we would distinguish a temporary adjustment from a preference that holds across similar tasks. The current physical control should always take precedence over an inferred preference.

A useful development check would alternate routine tasks with exceptions. Compare a version that adapts with one that keeps fixed settings. Count both the adjustments it saves and the new corrections it causes.

Then change the person's routine. Check whether the device can stop relying on an old pattern without making the owner reset the whole product.

An agent under the hood should reduce the need to repeat yourself while remaining easy to correct. All of that should happen locally, through the object itself.

Our first utility is in development. These are proposed checks, and the delicate-object example is illustrative.

title: Offline from the first use
body:
Working offline should include the first use.

Suppose a utility can do its job without a connection, but only after you create an account and download its model. The setup still depends on an outside service.

For v/h, the core capability should be ready on the device when it reaches its owner. That includes the local model and the tools it needs to act and check the result.

A proposed development check: take a unit in its shipped state and keep it offline from the moment it is opened. Give someone the included instructions. Can they finish the first core task without a phone, account or download?

If a physical adjustment or calibration is necessary, the device should guide it locally and make readiness clear. Record every point where the person needs outside help.

An update could improve the product later. It should not be required to make the basic job work for the first time.

Our first utility is in development. This is a requirement to prove before release.

title: Keep the result useful without the device
body:
A file made by a device should remain useful after the device is gone.

Imagine a physical utility that captures an everyday measurement. If the result can only be read inside a company app, the owner still depends on that company to use it.

We would want the result to leave the device in a format other tools can open. A saved measurement also needs its units and enough context to make sense later. Exporting an unexplained number would leave part of the job unfinished.

A useful development check would be to transfer the result locally, disconnect the utility, and open the file on a computer with no v/h software or account. Then check that the person can understand and reuse it.

An agent inside the product could interpret the inputs and check the result. Owning that result should not require access to the agent's internal software.

For v/h, independent ownership includes the useful output. Our first utility is in development. The measurement example is illustrative, not a product announcement.

What's a useful result you've struggled to get out of a device you own?

title: Count the hands a task takes
body:
One button can still take two hands.

Imagine a small utility that slides across the table when you press Start. Your other hand has to steady it. If that hand is already holding the object, even beginning the task becomes awkward.

For v/h, we want to count the physical adjustments an owner has to make. During setup, use and removal, we would record every moment someone has to brace the device, change their grip or ask for help.

We would try the sequence with either hand and with people who have different hand sizes and grip strength. The force needed to use a control belongs in the design, alongside its label and position.

An agent under the hood could handle repeated adjustments during the job. The controls and housing still have to work with the person using them.

Our first utility is in development. The document describes an imagined example and proposed checks, with the aim of making a new capability easier to use in an ordinary routine.

title: Design for the part that wears out
body:
A worn pad shouldn't make an otherwise working device disposable.

Consider an imagined utility that holds an object while doing a task. Suppose the contact pad wears out first. We would want to design its replacement alongside the original part.

The owner needs to be able to identify the part, find an affordable replacement and fit it safely. The attachment should make correct placement clear, including when the part is not fully seated.

After replacement, the product should have a clear way to check readiness. If the task requires calibration, we would want it to happen locally with understandable feedback.

An agent could help check whether the device is ready for use. It still needs suitable inputs, and the physical design needs to make routine maintenance straightforward.

For v/h, attainable cost includes the parts and effort needed to keep a utility working. Our first product is in development. The pad is an illustrative example of an upkeep requirement we have yet to prove.

title: Test the utility where it will be used
body:
The room shouldn't need to be arranged around the device.

For a utility that uses a camera, a shadow across the work area could change what it can see. Asking the owner to find the right lamp each time would add work to an ordinary task.

A useful development check would keep the task fixed while changing one condition at a time. Try it beside a window, in evening light, and with the object turned a different way. Record the result and every adjustment the person has to make.

If the device needs consistent lighting, we should account for it in the physical design. A built-in light or a different viewing angle may be part of the solution. A larger model still has to work with the information the device can actually capture.

For v/h, the local agent and the object around it need to be designed together. The owner should be able to use a new capability in an ordinary setting with familiar controls.

The camera example is illustrative. Our first utility is still in development, and dependable use in ordinary conditions is a requirement we have to prove.

title: Make the task status clear after the beep
body:
You shouldn't have to catch a beep to know whether a task finished.

Imagine leaving a utility running while you step into another room. When you return, the sound is over. You still need to know whether the job finished, stopped early, or needs your help.

For v/h, we want the task status to remain understandable after the sound stops. A short label such as "Finished" could accompany a light. Color and sound could draw attention, while the label preserves the meaning.

We would check the interface with sound muted and its colors shown in grayscale. Then we would ask someone returning to the device to explain its state and their next step, without coaching.

A local agent may handle a complicated task, but the owner should not need to watch closely to understand the outcome.

The example describes a design requirement for our first utility, which is still in development.

title: Decide what the device should remember
body:
A device should have a reason to remember the last task.

Imagine a local agent using an image to work out where an object is. It may need that image to act and check the result. Keeping the image after the job is a separate decision.

For v/h, we want to distinguish the inputs needed for a task from preferences that help with the next use. Remembering a chosen setting could save repeated setup. Saving a record of every task needs its own justification.

We would want to specify what is stored, why it is needed and when it is cleared. The owner should have an understandable way to clear personal task data without losing the device's core capability.

A development check would be to complete a task, clear the saved personal data, and try the core job again. We would inspect what remains on the device as well as what the interface says was cleared.

The document uses an imagined example to explain requirements for our first utility, which is still in development.

#ProductDesign #ConsumerTechnology

title: Choose the computing budget around the job
body:
Before choosing a larger model, we should be able to name the extra work it will do for the owner.

Imagine two versions of a utility that do the same job locally. One handles an awkward case on its own. The other needs the person to reposition an item and press Start again.

We would want to know how often the case comes up and how much effort the adjustment takes. Avoiding a repeated interruption could justify more expensive hardware. Solving a rare inconvenience might not.

A useful comparison would run both versions on hardware that fits the intended product, using the same ordinary tasks. We would count completed jobs and requests for help, including the time the person spends responding.

For v/h, the computing budget belongs alongside the product's price, power use and size from the start. Moving the core work to an online service would leave our requirement for local operation unproven.

The example is illustrative. Our first utility is still in development, with attainable cost and local operation as requirements we have to prove.

#ProductDesign #ConsumerTechnology

title: Compare the new device with the existing workaround
body:
A workaround is evidence of a need. It isn't evidence that people want another device.

Imagine someone using a folded towel to keep an object from sliding. A new device might hold it more firmly, but take longer to get out and clean. The towel is already nearby and useful for other things.

Before replacing a routine, we need to understand what it already does well.

For v/h, a useful comparison would start with the same person doing the same task in their usual setting. We would compare the result and the effort, including getting ready for the next use. The cost of owning the new device belongs in that comparison too.

The local agent needs to make a meaningful difference within the job. We should be able to explain which repeated decisions or difficult variations it handles, and how the owner benefits.

The towel example is illustrative, not a product announcement. Our first utility is still in development. We want evidence that a new capability improves the routine enough to justify another object.

title: The owner should have a direct way to stop
body:
A Stop button should not depend on a conversation with an AI.

Imagine starting a device, then noticing you put the wrong item in. You should be able to stop the task without opening an app or explaining your change of plan.

For v/h, we want the owner's direct controls to take priority over the agent's plan. The model can adjust how it carries out an agreed task. It should not decide whether a clear request to stop is worth following.

The feedback needs equal care. A device may need time to finish stopping a mechanism. It should distinguish "stopping" from "stopped," so someone knows what is still happening.

A useful development check would be to press Stop while the model is busy, then observe both the mechanism and the feedback. Does the control still work as intended?

We're treating direct control as a design requirement for our first utility, which is still in development. More decisions handled inside the product should leave the owner with a clear way to change their mind.

#ProductDesign #ConsumerTechnology

title: Design the action and the check together
body:
A device can follow an instruction and still leave the job unfinished.

Imagine a device meant to move an object. The motor turns, but the object slips and stays where it was. A record of the motor running would tell us very little about whether the task succeeded.

For v/h, an agent under the hood needs feedback about the result it is meant to produce. A local model should use the device's inputs to check what happened after acting through its tools.

During design, we want to identify an observation that distinguishes success from an attempted action.

The check should help determine the hardware, the software and what the owner sees. If the device cannot verify the result, it should communicate that uncertainty.

The document uses an imagined task to explain the requirement. Our first utility is still in development.

title: Usable by the person who did not set it up
body:
The person who didn't set it up should be able to use it.

Imagine a device on a shared kitchen counter. One person prefers a different result and changes a setting. The next person presses Start.

They should be able to see what will happen before the device begins.

For v/h, familiar controls have to include understandable settings. A preference saved by one person shouldn't become a surprise for the next.

A useful check during development would be to hand the product to someone who hasn't seen the demo. Explain its purpose, then see whether they can start the core job and recognize the outcome without coaching.

We want the agent to adapt how the work gets done while keeping the intended result under the user's control.

We're treating shared use as a design requirement for our first utility, which is still in development.

#ProductDesign #ConsumerTechnology

title: Count the whole job
body:
Count the work after "done."

Imagine a device that saves three minutes on a task, then adds five minutes of cleanup. The main action got faster, but the whole routine got longer.

For v/h, usefulness has to include setup, cleanup and upkeep. A result can be good while the product is still too much work to own.

We want to compare the owner's total effort with the way they already do the job. That includes getting the product ready for next time.

An agent under the hood has to earn its place in that comparison. Added capability should come with a manageable routine.

Our first utility is in development. Manageable upkeep is a design requirement we still have to prove in use.

What device do you use less often because cleaning it is too much work?

title: What an interrupted task should tell you
body:
If a device stops halfway through a task, 'Try again' isn't enough.

Imagine pressing Start and coming back to a device that has gone silent. You can't tell how much it finished, or whether starting again will repeat work it has already done.

For v/h, recovering from an interruption belongs in the design from the start. The owner should be able to tell:

• What finished.
• What still needs attention.
• What will happen if they try again.

The agent inside should check the current state before repeating an action. It needs evidence of the result before the product marks a task complete. When it can't verify what happened, the product should explain the uncertainty and give the owner a clear next step.

A simple control is only part of a simple experience. We also want someone to understand what to do after an interrupted job, without having to diagnose the software inside.

We're treating recovery as a design requirement while developing our first everyday utility.

What's an error message on a device you own that still leaves you unsure what to do next?

#ProductDesign #ConsumerTechnology

title: Less time managing the product
body:
A useful device can succeed by giving you fewer reasons to interact with it.

For an everyday utility, we care about whether the job gets done and how much effort the owner has to spend. Time spent setting it up, checking its output, or recovering from an error is part of that effort.

We want a person to start a task, understand the outcome, and get on with their day. A clear control and understandable feedback should make the product comfortable to use, even when the capability inside is new.

An agent earns its place when it helps deliver that experience.

We're developing our first utility around this standard. Follow v/h as we work through the choices needed to make it useful in everyday life.

#ConsumerTechnology #ProductDesign

title: What an everyday utility has to prove
body:
We want to judge our first utility by an ordinary week of use.

A successful demonstration gives us a starting point. Repeated use has to show that the product handles normal variation, completes the job, and communicates clearly when it can't.

Our development questions cover the whole experience. The task needs to recur. The controls need to make sense. The result needs to be dependable. Price and upkeep need to fit the people the product is for.

We also want to understand how much checking the owner has to do. A device that repeatedly needs someone to verify or redo its work can give effort back to the person it was meant to help.

The document below sets out the standard we're working toward. It describes what we need to establish through development, rather than results from a finished product.

title: The core function belongs with the product
body:
You should be able to use the core function of a product you own without keeping a service running.

For v/h, that means designing the computing needed for the job into the device itself.

Our aim is straightforward. Power it on and use it without an account, a companion app, an internet connection, or a subscription.

Local operation creates engineering constraints around cost, power, size, and performance. We have to solve those constraints as part of making the product useful. A prototype that depends on a cloud service for its essential work would leave that part of our philosophy unproven.

Each v/h utility should also stand on its own. Buying one should give you a useful capability without requiring the rest of an ecosystem.

These are design requirements for our first product, which is still in development.

title: Made to be useful
body:
You shouldn't have to be interested in technology to benefit from it.

v/h is building a new kind of everyday consumer utility. We want to give people a useful capability through a physical product whose purpose and controls feel familiar.

The starting point is a common, recurring need. An agent inside the device should handle the complicated work, so the person using it can get a clear result with less effort.

We're designing the core function to work locally, without an account, companion app, internet connection, or subscription.

Our first utility is in development. It has to earn a place in an ordinary day through usefulness, simplicity, and dependable results.

Follow v/h for the product decisions and tradeoffs behind that work.

title: What we mean by an agent under the hood
body:
The complicated decisions should happen inside the product.

For v/h, an agent under the hood means a local model connected to the device's inputs and tools. It can interpret the task, act through those tools, and check what happened.

The owner should have a clear way to start the job and understand the result. They shouldn't need to choose a model, write a prompt, or troubleshoot the agent's reasoning.

The agent also has to justify the cost and complexity it adds. We would look for a better result, less effort from the owner, or the ability to handle ordinary variation that a simpler mechanism cannot.

The document below explains the product principle we're building around.

title: Easy to use and useful to many people
body:
A product can be easy for everyone to use and still be useful to almost no one.

Ease of use and breadth of need are separate requirements. At v/h, we want both.

A clear button can make a device understandable. The job behind that button still needs to come up often enough for people to want the device in their lives.

We start with recurring tasks and the workarounds people already use. Then we have to establish whether a new physical utility would make those tasks easier.

The ambition is a product that earns its place through repeated use. A narrow, clearly defined job can be relevant to a very large number of people.

What's a small task you keep repeating because the current way of doing it is still inconvenient? A specific example would help us understand the need.

#ConsumerTechnology #ProductDesign
